holdings_chronological.title: Accounts Officer, Jharkhand State Electricity Board v. Anwar Ali
holdings_chronological.holding: Supply of electric energy by the utility falls within 'service' as defined in Section 2(o) of the Consumer Protection Act, 1986.

holdings_chronological.title: M/s Prem Cottex v. Uttar Haryana Bijli Vitran Nigam Ltd.
holdings_chronological.holding: Raising a short-assessment demand to correct the licensee's own wrong multiply-factor is not a 'deficiency in service' where the consumer does not dispute the short-billing; it is 'escaped assessment', so the consumer fora cannot interfere.

holdings_chronological.title: K.C. Ninan v. Kerala State Electricity Board
holdings_chronological.holding: The duty to supply electricity under Section 43 is not absolute; it is subject to the charges and compliances stipulated by the electric utilities as part of the application for supply.

holdings_chronological.title: K.C. Ninan v. Kerala State Electricity Board
holdings_chronological.holding: The Section 43 duty is owed with respect to the owner/occupier of the premises (a consumer-premises synergy); one becomes a consumer only with respect to the particular premises for which electricity is sought and provided.

holdings_chronological.title: Bihar State Electricity Board v. Kishori Devi
holdings_chronological.holding: Consumption beyond the sanctioned load without the Board's consent amounts to theft or malpractice; the statutory tariff (Clause 16.9) empowers the Board to disconnect supply without notice on detecting unauthorised load.

holdings_chronological.title: K.C. Ninan v. Kerala State Electricity Board
holdings_chronological.holding: A Condition of Supply requiring a new owner to clear the previous owner's electricity arrears as a precondition to supply has a statutory character.

holdings_chronological.title: K.C. Ninan v. Kerala State Electricity Board
holdings_chronological.holding: The State Commission's regulatory powers under Section 50 are wide enough to stipulate conditions for recovery of a previous owner's electricity arrears from new or subsequent owners.

holdings_chronological.title: K.C. Ninan v. Kerala State Electricity Board
holdings_chronological.holding: The rule-making power under Section 181 read with Section 50 is wide enough to enable the regulatory commission to provide for a statutory CHARGE on the premises, even absent a charge-creating provision in the plenary statute.

holdings_chronological.title: Sandeep Kesarwani v. State of U.P. & 3 Others
holdings_chronological.holding: Electricity dues under a Section 126 assessment become 'first due' for Section 56(2) only when the final assessment is made — not on the date of detection or consumption; the two-year bar runs from the final assessment, so recovery initiated soon after it is within time.

holdings_chronological.title: Assistant Engineer (D1), Ajmer Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Rahamatullah Khan
holdings_chronological.holding: Electricity charges become 'first due' under Section 56(2) only after the bill is issued to the consumer, even though the liability to pay arises on consumption; the obligation to pay arises when the bill quantifying the charges is issued.

holdings_chronological.title: Assistant Engineer (D1), Ajmer Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Rahamatullah Khan
holdings_chronological.holding: Section 56(1) confers a statutory right on the licensee to disconnect supply for non-payment; that right is subject to the two-year limitation in Section 56(2).

holdings_chronological.title: Assistant Engineer (D1), Ajmer Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Rahamatullah Khan
holdings_chronological.holding: The two-year period runs from when the charges became first due; Section 56(2) restricts the licensee's right to disconnect for non-payment unless the sum has been shown continuously as recoverable arrears in the bills for the past period.

holdings_chronological.title: Assistant Engineer (D1), Ajmer Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Rahamatullah Khan
holdings_chronological.holding: Section 56(2) bars ONLY the coercive remedy of disconnection after two years; it does not preclude the licensee from raising a supplementary demand or pursuing other modes of recovery for it.

holdings_chronological.title: Assistant Engineer (D1), Ajmer Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Rahamatullah Khan
holdings_chronological.holding: In case of a bona fide mistake, the licensee may raise an additional/supplementary demand after the two-year period, but cannot take recourse to disconnection to recover it (limitation for a suit running from discovery of the mistake under Section 17(1)(c) of the Limitation Act).

holdings_chronological.title: M/s Prem Cottex v. Uttar Haryana Bijli Vitran Nigam Ltd.
holdings_chronological.holding: The Section 56(2) bar is not merely on disconnection of supply but also on recovery; it operates on two distinct rights of the licensee — the right to recover and the right to disconnect.

holdings_chronological.title: M/s Prem Cottex v. Uttar Haryana Bijli Vitran Nigam Ltd.
holdings_chronological.holding: The second part of Section 56(2) is an exception to the general law of limitation, which normally bars only the remedy (through a court) and not the right — here it bars even the remedy of disconnection.

holdings_chronological.title: M/s Prem Cottex v. Uttar Haryana Bijli Vitran Nigam Ltd.
holdings_chronological.holding: Section 56 is keyed to a consumer's neglect to pay a charge; the licensee's own negligence causing short-billing, and its later rectification, is not covered by Section 56(1), so such a corrective claim may not attract the Section 56(2) 'no sum due from any consumer' bar.

holdings_chronological.title: M/s Prem Cottex v. Uttar Haryana Bijli Vitran Nigam Ltd.
holdings_chronological.holding: The question of neglect to pay arises only after a demand is raised; if no bill is raised, limitation under Section 56(2) does not begin to run, and until it runs the bar on recovery/disconnection does not operate.

holdings_chronological.title: K.C. Ninan v. Kerala State Electricity Board
holdings_chronological.holding: The power to initiate recovery proceedings by filing a suit against a defaulting consumer is independent of the power to disconnect supply as a means of recovery under Section 56.

holdings_chronological.title: Hasi Mazumdar v. West Bengal State Electricity Board
holdings_chronological.holding: Money paid pursuant to an illegal assessment under the threat that supply would not be restored until payment is recoverable; allowing the Board to retain it would be unjust enrichment impermissible under the Contract Act.

holdings_chronological.title: Assessing Officer-cum-Executive Engineer (Electrical), WESCO v. Appellate Authority-cum-Electrical Inspector
holdings_chronological.holding: Section 125 (appeal to the Supreme Court from the Appellate Tribunal, Part XI) and Section 127 (appeal to the appellate authority from a Section 126 assessment, Part XII) are totally different and operate in different contexts; authority on Section 125 limitation does not govern a Section 127 appeal.

holdings_chronological.title: Hasi Mazumdar v. West Bengal State Electricity Board
holdings_chronological.holding: From the commencement of the Electricity Act, 2003 (10.6.2003), a provisional assessment for unauthorised use must be made strictly in accordance with Section 126; an assessment made under the Board's old Terms & Conditions of Supply (Clause 22(J)) is not in accordance with Section 126 and is bad.

holdings_chronological.title: Hasi Mazumdar v. West Bengal State Electricity Board
holdings_chronological.holding: Section 126(1) requires the assessing officer to provisionally assess 'to the best of his judgment' on his own personal observation of the extent of unauthorised use; this quasi-judicial function cannot be fettered by a superior's guideline/office order — an assessment dictated by such a direction is the direction-giver's judgment, not the officer's, and is illegal.

holdings_chronological.title: Hasi Mazumdar v. West Bengal State Electricity Board
holdings_chronological.holding: On the facts, the assessment was not the officer's judgment but the judgment of those who issued the 30.12.2003 guideline, and was therefore not an impartial or legal assessment (evidenced by an absurd quantum ~6 times the consumer's highest average consumption).

holdings_chronological.title: Hasi Mazumdar v. West Bengal State Electricity Board
holdings_chronological.holding: Money paid pursuant to an illegal assessment under the threat that supply would not be restored until payment is recoverable; allowing the Board to retain it would be unjust enrichment impermissible under the Contract Act.

holdings_chronological.title: Harvinder Motors v. BSES Rajdhani Power Ltd.
holdings_chronological.holding: An assessment for unauthorised use / DAE must be preceded by inspection and a reasonable hearing; the licensee is bound by the principles of natural justice (Section 126(3) read with Reg. 25(viii)).

holdings_chronological.title: Harvinder Motors v. BSES Rajdhani Power Ltd.
holdings_chronological.holding: A suspicion of unauthorised use / DAE must be corroborated by the consumer's consumption pattern; that corroboration is a precondition to the exercise of assessment jurisdiction, and where consumption exceeds ~75% of the assessed figure no action can be taken. A missing seal or broken glass alone will not do.

holdings_chronological.title: Harvinder Motors v. BSES Rajdhani Power Ltd.
holdings_chronological.holding: The show-cause notice must precisely and unambiguously state the allegations on which action is proposed; a notice that keeps the real basis (here, the consumption-pattern / two-shift-use finding) from the consumer fails the standard of fairness.

holdings_chronological.title: Accounts Officer, Jharkhand State Electricity Board v. Anwar Ali
holdings_chronological.holding: Assessment of the charge for unauthorised use, meter-tampering and calibration are technical matters; whether the beneficial consumer jurisdiction extends to such determinations (and to tortious acts like disconnection) is left open and remitted to the National Commission.

holdings_chronological.title: Sh. B.L. Kantroo v. BSES Rajdhani Power Ltd.
holdings_chronological.holding: Section 126 excludes mens rea and fastens civil liability; unauthorised use of electricity is different from theft, which is a criminal offence under Section 135.

holdings_chronological.title: M/s Mohit Paper Mills Ltd. v. PVVNL
holdings_chronological.holding: The assessing officer has no jurisdiction to make a theft assessment unless he first establishes a case of theft against the person (para 8.1(b)(iv)); merely issuing a provisional assessment order does not establish theft.

holdings_chronological.title: M/s Mohit Paper Mills Ltd. v. PVVNL
holdings_chronological.holding: Theft of electrical energy cannot be made out on mere presumption; it has to be established as required by para 8.1(b)(iv) of the Code.

holdings_chronological.title: M/s Mohit Paper Mills Ltd. v. PVVNL
holdings_chronological.holding: A best-judgment assessment under Section 126 must be arrived at without bias and on a rational basis; the officer cannot take a 'short cut' by recording an evasive conclusion in the provisional assessment without discussing how the inference of unauthorised use/theft was reached.

holdings_chronological.title: M/s Mohit Paper Mills Ltd. v. PVVNL
holdings_chronological.holding: The law requires an opportunity of oral hearing to the consumer before final assessment; none was given here (no date was communicated for the consumer to answer the charges in person).

holdings_chronological.title: M/s Mohit Paper Mills Ltd. v. PVVNL
holdings_chronological.holding: Section 126 assessment may be made even on inspection of records where a person is found in unauthorised use, without attracting Section 135, because Section 135 contemplates a positive act interfering with the recording of electricity supplied.

holdings_chronological.title: Executive Engineer, Southern Electricity Supply Co. of Orissa Ltd. (SOUTHCO) v. Sri Seetaram Rice Mill
holdings_chronological.holding: Sections 126 and 135 are distinct provisions that operate in different and distinct fields and have no commonality in law.

holdings_chronological.title: Executive Engineer, Southern Electricity Supply Co. of Orissa Ltd. (SOUTHCO) v. Sri Seetaram Rice Mill
holdings_chronological.holding: Section 135 theft falls within criminal jurisprudence and mens rea is a relevant factor; Section 126 does not speak of any criminal intendment and is primarily a civil remedy without elements traceable to mens rea.

holdings_chronological.title: Executive Engineer, Southern Electricity Supply Co. of Orissa Ltd. (SOUTHCO) v. Sri Seetaram Rice Mill
holdings_chronological.holding: 'Unauthorised use of electricity' under Section 126 deals with cases of unauthorised use even in the absence of intention — distinct from dishonest abstraction under Section 135.

holdings_chronological.title: Executive Engineer, Southern Electricity Supply Co. of Orissa Ltd. (SOUTHCO) v. Sri Seetaram Rice Mill
holdings_chronological.holding: 'Unauthorised use of electricity' is an expression of wider connotation to be construed purposively; excess-load consumption beyond the connected load falls under Explanation (b)(iv) to Section 126 (besides violating the Regulations and agreement).

holdings_chronological.title: Executive Engineer, Southern Electricity Supply Co. of Orissa Ltd. (SOUTHCO) v. Sri Seetaram Rice Mill
holdings_chronological.holding: Sections 126 and 127 read together constitute a complete code; only a final order of assessment under Section 126(3) is appealable under Section 127, and a notice-cum-provisional assessment under Section 126(2) is not appealable.

holdings_chronological.title: Executive Engineer, Southern Electricity Supply Co. of Orissa Ltd. (SOUTHCO) v. Sri Seetaram Rice Mill
holdings_chronological.holding: The High Court should normally decline to interfere under Article 226 with a final assessment; it may examine a jurisdictional challenge but must not travel into the assessing officer's exclusive domain of assessment and fact-finding.

holdings_chronological.title: M/s Shyam Lal Iron & Steel Co. v. Jharkhand State Electricity Board
holdings_chronological.holding: Sections 126 and 135 sit in different Parts (XII vs XIV), cover different fields and prescribe different procedures; theft involves mens rea, which is not necessary for unauthorised use under Section 126.

holdings_chronological.title: M/s Shyam Lal Iron & Steel Co. v. Jharkhand State Electricity Board
holdings_chronological.holding: Labelling a theft demand as a 'Section 126 provisional assessment' does not convert a theft proceeding into a Section 126 assessment where, on the date of inspection, it was treated as theft (FIR lodged) and not even as suspected theft.

holdings_chronological.title: U.P. Power Corporation Ltd. & Ors. v. Anis Ahmad
holdings_chronological.holding: A final assessment under Section 126 for 'unauthorised use of electricity' is a quasi-judicial decision by a public servant; it is not a 'consumer dispute' under Section 2(1)(e) of the Consumer Protection Act, 1986, and cannot be challenged by a consumer complaint.

holdings_chronological.title: U.P. Power Corporation Ltd. & Ors. v. Anis Ahmad
holdings_chronological.holding: The same acts of 'unauthorised use of electricity' attract a civil consequence (penal assessment at twice the tariff) under Section 126 and simultaneously constitute offences under Sections 135–140 — the two operate in parallel on the same conduct.

holdings_chronological.title: Sandeep Kesarwani v. State of U.P. & 3 Others
holdings_chronological.holding: 'Unauthorised use of electricity' (s.126) is the genus of which the theft acts in s.135(1) are species; theft is unauthorised use done dishonestly. A Section 126 assessment therefore has to follow in every case of unauthorised use, including theft — neither section excludes the other.

holdings_chronological.title: Sandeep Kesarwani v. State of U.P. & 3 Others
holdings_chronological.holding: A final assessment must be passed within thirty days of the provisional order under Section 126(3); a final order passed about two years later, without a fresh opportunity of hearing, violates natural justice and cannot be sustained.

holdings_chronological.title: Ramesh Chand v. Uttar Haryana Bijli Vitran Nigam Ltd.
holdings_chronological.holding: Sections 126 and 135 operate in different fields: Section 126 is invoked for over-consumption / unauthorised use of electricity, whereas Section 135 is invoked for theft of electricity.

holdings_chronological.title: Ramesh Chand v. Uttar Haryana Bijli Vitran Nigam Ltd.
holdings_chronological.holding: Section 126 cannot be applied to assess the amount to be charged for theft of electricity; the civil liability for theft is measured under the Section 154(5) formula (twice the tariff for the twelve months preceding detection, or the exact period of theft if determined, whichever is less), subject to final adjudication by the Special Court.

holdings_chronological.title: Sulabha Marketing (P) Ltd. v. Kerala State Electricity Board
holdings_chronological.holding: The physical presence of the assessing officer at the time of inspection and detection of unauthorised use is not a mandatory precondition for initiating assessment proceedings under Section 126(1).

holdings_chronological.title: Sulabha Marketing (P) Ltd. v. Kerala State Electricity Board
holdings_chronological.holding: 'Unauthorised use of electricity' under Section 126 covers cases of unauthorised use even without intention; the consumer's intention is not the foundation for an assessment order under Section 126 (mens rea is a Section 135 concept).

holdings_chronological.title: Sulabha Marketing (P) Ltd. v. Kerala State Electricity Board
holdings_chronological.holding: A consumer who consumes electricity in excess of the sanctioned/connected load (breach of the agreement, Regulations and the Act) is liable to pay at the rate equal to twice the tariff applicable for the relevant category of services.

holdings_chronological.title: Sulabha Marketing (P) Ltd. v. Kerala State Electricity Board
holdings_chronological.holding: The word 'tariff' in Section 126(6) includes BOTH fixed charges and energy charges; the assessment is at twice that tariff for the relevant category of services under sub-section (5).

holdings_chronological.title: Sulabha Marketing (P) Ltd. v. Kerala State Electricity Board
holdings_chronological.holding: Where electricity of one category is unauthorisedly used for a higher-tariff purpose, the assessment is twice the tariff applicable to that higher-tariff category for which it was used — not twice the tariff of the category to which the consumer nominally belongs.

holdings_chronological.title: Sulabha Marketing (P) Ltd. v. Kerala State Electricity Board
holdings_chronological.holding: MARQUEE EXCEPTION: where the consumer is only blamed with overdrawal in excess of sanctioned/connected load in the same premises and for the same purpose (no change in the tariff category), and the excess consumption has already been metered and paid, the assessment under Section 126(6) can only be twice the FIXED charges — the consumer cannot be saddled with twice the energy charges — unless regularising the additional load necessitates upgradation of the distribution system or enhancement of the voltage level.

holdings_chronological.title: Shishir Jain v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd.
holdings_chronological.holding: The condition precedent to a provisional assessment under Section 126(1) is a conclusion by the Assessing Officer that the person is indulging in unauthorised use; that satisfaction cannot rest on the officer's mere 'vagaries' without a fair opportunity of hearing in defence.

holdings_chronological.title: Shishir Jain v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd.
holdings_chronological.holding: Principles of natural justice apply to proceedings for unauthorised use of electricity (which may in some cases also amount to an investigation under Section 135) unless excluded by the Act expressly or by necessary implication.

holdings_chronological.title: Shishir Jain v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd.
holdings_chronological.holding: A final assessment made without considering the consumer's objections and without a personal hearing (as required by Section 126(3) and Clause 8.1(b)(iii) of the 2005 Code) is dehors the statutory provision and cannot stand.

holdings_chronological.title: Shishir Jain v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd.
holdings_chronological.holding: Absent a lawful final assessment made after considering objections and hearing, the consumer cannot be compelled to deposit the provisional amount.

holdings_chronological.title: Assessing Officer-cum-Executive Engineer (Electrical), WESCO v. Appellate Authority-cum-Electrical Inspector
holdings_chronological.holding: An inspection alleging unauthorised use under Section 126 should be conducted in the presence of the consumer (a signatory to the inspection report); the licensee's failure to show the night inspection was in the consumer's presence undermined its case.

holdings_chronological.title: Assessing Officer-cum-Executive Engineer (Electrical), WESCO v. Appellate Authority-cum-Electrical Inspector
holdings_chronological.holding: The Section 126(5) 12-month cap applies only where the period of unauthorised use is not ascertainable; where the period is ascertained (as here, and reduced by the Appellate Authority), the assessment is confined to that ascertained period.

holdings_chronological.title: V. Swaminathan v. Superintending Engineer, TANGEDCO
holdings_chronological.holding: Section 135 theft falls within criminal jurisprudence and mens rea is the relevant factor; Section 126 (read with the Supply Code) does not speak of criminal intent, and the assessment under it is appealable under Section 127, whereas a Section 135 assessment (Reg. 23-AA) has no statutory appeal.

holdings_chronological.title: M/s Jindal Resources Pvt. Ltd. v. Executive Engineer (Elect.), WESCO
holdings_chronological.holding: A Section 135 criminal proceeding has no bearing on a Section 126 proceeding; even an acquittal in the criminal case for a Section 135 offence does not exonerate the consumer from Section 126 civil liability.

holdings_chronological.title: M/s Jindal Resources Pvt. Ltd. v. Executive Engineer (Elect.), WESCO
holdings_chronological.holding: Seetaram Rice Mill lays down no ratio that a Section 126 assessment cannot be undertaken in theft cases; Section 126 covers cases over and above Section 135, and the two must be read harmoniously to make both effective.

holdings_chronological.title: West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd. (WBSEDCL) v. M/s Orion Metal Pvt. Ltd.
holdings_chronological.holding: All instances of unauthorised use may not amount to theft, but theft under Section 135 falls within the definition of 'unauthorised use of electricity'; hence use through a tampered meter (Section 126(6)(b)(iii)) is unauthorised use assessable under Section 126.

holdings_chronological.title: West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd. (WBSEDCL) v. M/s Orion Metal Pvt. Ltd.
holdings_chronological.holding: The authorities are empowered to make a provisional and final assessment under Section 126(1) even in cases where electricity is unauthorisedly used by way of theft.

holdings_chronological.title: West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd. (WBSEDCL) v. M/s Orion Metal Pvt. Ltd.
holdings_chronological.holding: The Section 126(1) assessment power and the Section 154(5) Special Court power to determine civil liability are not parallel to each other; the High Court erred in holding that both proceedings cannot operate parallelly.

holdings_chronological.title: West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd. (WBSEDCL) v. M/s Orion Metal Pvt. Ltd.
holdings_chronological.holding: Where there is no theft (only unauthorised use), no Section 135 complaint lies and the loss is assessed under Section 126(1); where the unauthorised use amounts to theft, a Section 126(1) assessment AND a Section 135 complaint may both proceed, with the Special Court determining civil liability under Section 154(5) and any excess deposit refunded.

holdings_chronological.title: West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd. (WBSEDCL) v. M/s Orion Metal Pvt. Ltd.
holdings_chronological.holding: To prove theft in a criminal proceeding, the case must be proved beyond reasonable doubt with mens rea established; such strict proof is not necessary for assessing liability under Section 126(1).

holdings_chronological.title: Rakesh Singh v. State of U.P.
holdings_chronological.holding: Unauthorised use of electricity (Explanation (b) to Section 126) is the genus of which the Section 135(1) acts are species; theft is unauthorised use done dishonestly, so a Section 126 assessment must follow whenever there is unauthorised use.

holdings_chronological.title: Rakesh Singh v. State of U.P.
holdings_chronological.holding: Neither Section 126 nor Section 135 excludes a Section 126 assessment where the unauthorised use amounts to theft; the sixth proviso to Section 135(1) itself speaks of the 'assessed amount', i.e. the amount assessed under Section 126.

holdings_chronological.title: Rakesh Singh v. State of U.P.
holdings_chronological.holding: A Section 126 assessment is to be made even where an offence under Section 135 has been made out (FIR/final report notwithstanding); the Special Court finally determines the civil liability, with further action under Section 154(6).

holdings_chronological.title: Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd. v. M/s Shubhalaxmi Rice Mill
holdings_chronological.holding: Consumption in excess of the sanctioned contract demand, causing a change of tariff category (LT to HT), is 'unauthorised use of electricity' squarely covered by Explanation (b)(iv) to Section 126; the consumers' cases stood clearly covered under Section 126.

holdings_chronological.title: Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd. v. M/s Shubhalaxmi Rice Mill
holdings_chronological.holding: Following Seetaram Rice Mill (para 35), intention is not the foundation for invoking Section 126; all that need be ascertained is whether the consumer exceeded the contract load resulting in usage beyond it.

holdings_chronological.title: Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd. v. M/s Shubhalaxmi Rice Mill
holdings_chronological.holding: Even where penalty @150% has already been levied for exceeding the contract demand under the Regulatory Commission's tariff order, the consumer remains liable to pay charges for unauthorised use of electricity under Section 126.

holdings_chronological.title: Hasimuddin v. State of U.P.
holdings_chronological.holding: Even where an FIR is lodged under Section 135, the assessment is carried out under Section 126 (with the Section 127 appeal remedy), and the Special Court finally determines the civil liability under Section 154(6).

holdings_chronological.title: Ashok Kumar Maity v. West Bengal State Electricity Board (WBSEDCL)
holdings_chronological.holding: Unauthorised use of electricity (Section 126) is the genus and theft (Section 135) is one of the species thereunder; the two operate in different fields.

holdings_chronological.title: Ashok Kumar Maity v. West Bengal State Electricity Board (WBSEDCL)
holdings_chronological.holding: A Section 126 assessment is a civil enquiry to be decided on the standard of preponderance of probability, whereas Section 135 theft requires proof beyond reasonable doubt with mens rea; the yardsticks are distinct.

holdings_chronological.title: Ashok Kumar Maity v. West Bengal State Electricity Board (WBSEDCL)
holdings_chronological.holding: An acquittal on a Section 135 theft charge (tested on proof beyond reasonable doubt) does not ipso facto exonerate the consumer from civil liability under Section 126 (tested on the more liberal preponderance of probability).

holdings_chronological.title: Tapan Sen Majumdar v. West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd.
holdings_chronological.holding: Sections 126 and 135 operate in separate fields and parallel proceedings may run; Section 126 is civil (preponderance of probability), Section 135 is criminal (beyond reasonable doubt) — the standards of proof differ.

holdings_chronological.title: Tapan Sen Majumdar v. West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd.
holdings_chronological.holding: Where a tampered/bypassed meter is the ONLY allegation and it founds both the Section 135 prosecution and the Section 126 assessment (self-same allegation), an acquittal scot-free in the criminal case means the consumer cannot be indicted for the same charge even on a preponderance of probability.

holdings_chronological.title: Tapan Sen Majumdar v. West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd.
holdings_chronological.holding: It is the incumbent duty of the licensee to pass a final order of assessment within 30 days of service of the provisional assessment, even if the consumer files no objection.

holdings_chronological.title: Tapan Sen Majumdar v. West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd.
holdings_chronological.holding: If no final order is drawn up, the provisional assessment order spends its force after 30 days from its service on the consumer.

holdings_chronological.title: Castron Technologies Ltd. v. Damodar Valley Corporation
holdings_chronological.holding: The contention that an acquittal in the Section 135 criminal case extinguishes Section 126 liability is not acceptable — a Section 135 proceeding has no bearing on a Section 126 proceeding (following Orion Metal and Seetaram Rice Mill).

holdings_chronological.title: Castron Technologies Ltd. v. Damodar Valley Corporation
holdings_chronological.holding: The provisional assessment must be supplied to the consumer under Section 126(2); in the absence of such service there should be no demand, because a statutory power must be exercised only in the manner prescribed and not otherwise.

holdings_chronological.title: Castron Technologies Ltd. v. Damodar Valley Corporation
holdings_chronological.holding: A decision under Section 126 must be taken strictly in accordance with the statutory provision — when a statute provides that a thing be done in a particular manner, it must be done in that manner and not in any other.

holdings_chronological.title: Castron Technologies Ltd. v. Damodar Valley Corporation
holdings_chronological.holding: A demand issued without considering the consumer's objection and without making a final assessment requires interference and must be remitted for a fresh decision strictly per Section 126.

holdings_chronological.title: Md. Abdul Matin v. West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd.
holdings_chronological.holding: The vires of Sections 126 and 135 is upheld; the overlap on tampering creates no double standards — where both theft and unauthorised-use ingredients are satisfied, the authorities may make a Section 126 assessment AND proceed with a Section 135 criminal trial before the Special Court.

holdings_chronological.title: Md. Abdul Matin v. West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd.
holdings_chronological.holding: No hearing is required before a provisional assessment under Section 126(1) (which is not conclusive); the right of hearing and to file objections is given before the final order, and requiring a hearing before the provisional assessment would defeat the summary, expeditious timeline.

holdings_chronological.title: Md. Abdul Matin v. West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd.
holdings_chronological.holding: The assessing officer is a State Government appointee (whether of the Government or the licensee) and so has an independent character, not functioning merely as an employee of the licensee — hence no unbridled power and no basis to strike down the Section.

holdings_chronological.title: Md. Abdul Matin v. West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd.
holdings_chronological.holding: A Section 126 finding does not indict a person of theft (a criminal charge); the assessing officer merely calculates the licensee's loss, and whether theft is established is left to the Special Court's full criminal trial — so no violation of Articles 19/21.

holdings_chronological.title: Executive Engineer, Southern Electricity Supply Co. of Orissa Ltd. (SOUTHCO) v. Sri Seetaram Rice Mill
holdings_chronological.holding: Sections 126 and 127 read together constitute a complete code; only a final order of assessment under Section 126(3) is appealable under Section 127, and a notice-cum-provisional assessment under Section 126(2) is not appealable.

holdings_chronological.title: M/s Shyam Lal Iron & Steel Co. v. Jharkhand State Electricity Board
holdings_chronological.holding: The Section 127 appeal lies only against a Section 126 order, not against a Section 135(1A)/Clause 15.8 theft assessment; the latter is examinable by the Special Court under Section 154(5)/(6).

holdings_chronological.title: U.P. Power Corporation Ltd. & Ors. v. Anis Ahmad
holdings_chronological.holding: The remedy against a final Section 126 order is an appeal to the appellate authority under Section 127, entertained only on deposit of half the assessed amount; the appellate order is final.

holdings_chronological.title: Sandeep Kesarwani v. State of U.P. & 3 Others
holdings_chronological.holding: A Section 126 final assessment in a theft case is appealable under Section 127 (following Paliwal Alloys); a writ was nonetheless entertained here because jurisdiction was challenged and the order breached natural justice.

holdings_chronological.title: Assessing Officer-cum-Executive Engineer (Electrical), WESCO v. Appellate Authority-cum-Electrical Inspector
holdings_chronological.holding: A Section 127 appeal is not barred by limitation where the delay is attributable to the consumer's bona fide pursuit of a writ petition and writ appeal in the wrong forum; Section 14 of the Limitation Act applies to exclude that period (the Electricity Act being a special law under Section 29(2) that does not expressly exclude Section 14).

holdings_chronological.title: Assessing Officer-cum-Executive Engineer (Electrical), WESCO v. Appellate Authority-cum-Electrical Inspector
holdings_chronological.holding: Section 125 (appeal to the Supreme Court from the Appellate Tribunal, Part XI) and Section 127 (appeal to the appellate authority from a Section 126 assessment, Part XII) are totally different and operate in different contexts; authority on Section 125 limitation does not govern a Section 127 appeal.

holdings_chronological.title: V. Swaminathan v. Superintending Engineer, TANGEDCO
holdings_chronological.holding: An appellate order rejecting a Section 127 appeal as not maintainable, passed without affording any opportunity of hearing, warrants interference and is quashed and remitted.

holdings_chronological.title: M/s Jindal Resources Pvt. Ltd. v. Executive Engineer (Elect.), WESCO
holdings_chronological.holding: Where no Section 127 appeal is filed against the final Section 126 assessment, it attains finality and the consumer is liable to pay the assessed amount.

holdings_chronological.title: Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd. v. M/s Shubhalaxmi Rice Mill
holdings_chronological.holding: Where the High Court has remanded a Section 127 appeal confined to quantum, the Appellate Authority cannot re-open the settled question whether Section 126 applies; the only question open to it is the quantum of assessment in the final bills.

holdings_chronological.title: Hasimuddin v. State of U.P.
holdings_chronological.holding: An order of assessment under Section 126 is appealable under Section 127 to the Commissioner of the Division (the notified appellate authority under the 14.7.2006 notification); the Commissioner was not justified in dismissing the appeal for want of jurisdiction.

holdings_chronological.title: Hasimuddin v. State of U.P.
holdings_chronological.holding: The State's 14.7.2006 notification confers on the Commissioner of the Division the power to hear and decide appeals under Section 127.

holdings_chronological.title: Ashok Kumar Maity v. West Bengal State Electricity Board (WBSEDCL)
holdings_chronological.holding: A consumer who bypasses the Section 127 appeal (which requires a 50% pre-deposit) cannot obtain from the writ court, indirectly, the restoration he could not get from the appellate forum; there is no unqualified restoration without complying with the final assessment.

holdings_chronological.title: Tapan Sen Majumdar v. West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd.
holdings_chronological.holding: No Section 127 appeal lay because no final order of assessment was ever made; hence the writ under Article 226 is maintainable.

holdings_chronological.title: Md. Abdul Matin v. West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd.
holdings_chronological.holding: The 50% mandatory pre-deposit under Section 127(2) is not exorbitant and is in consonance with the objects of the Act; a writ court will not sit in judgment under Article 226 over the propriety of the pre-deposit quantum.

holdings_chronological.title: Md. Abdul Matin v. West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd.
holdings_chronological.holding: The petitioners had long overshot the Section 127 limitation and taken direct writ recourse, with nothing in the assessments reeking of palpable arbitrariness or patent perversity — so no interference under Article 226 even on merits.

holdings_chronological.title: Hasi Mazumdar v. West Bengal State Electricity Board
holdings_chronological.holding: Even if hooking was found, the Board could de-hook, realise the value of unauthorised consumption at the penal rate, or proceed under Section 135 — but that did not authorise the disconnection effected or an illegal assessment.

holdings_chronological.title: M/s Mohit Paper Mills Ltd. v. PVVNL
holdings_chronological.holding: Section 126 assessment may be made even on inspection of records where a person is found in unauthorised use, without attracting Section 135, because Section 135 contemplates a positive act interfering with the recording of electricity supplied.

holdings_chronological.title: Executive Engineer, Southern Electricity Supply Co. of Orissa Ltd. (SOUTHCO) v. Sri Seetaram Rice Mill
holdings_chronological.holding: Sections 126 and 135 are distinct provisions that operate in different and distinct fields and have no commonality in law.

holdings_chronological.title: Executive Engineer, Southern Electricity Supply Co. of Orissa Ltd. (SOUTHCO) v. Sri Seetaram Rice Mill
holdings_chronological.holding: Section 135 theft falls within criminal jurisprudence and mens rea is a relevant factor; Section 126 does not speak of any criminal intendment and is primarily a civil remedy without elements traceable to mens rea.

holdings_chronological.title: M/s Shyam Lal Iron & Steel Co. v. Jharkhand State Electricity Board
holdings_chronological.holding: Sections 126 and 135 sit in different Parts (XII vs XIV), cover different fields and prescribe different procedures; theft involves mens rea, which is not necessary for unauthorised use under Section 126.

holdings_chronological.title: M/s Shyam Lal Iron & Steel Co. v. Jharkhand State Electricity Board
holdings_chronological.holding: A missing/tampered seal or broken glass window is not, by itself, evidence of theft unless corroborated by the consumer's consumption pattern and other available evidence — this is the safeguard for suspected-theft cases (Clause 15.8(x)-(xv)).

holdings_chronological.title: U.P. Power Corporation Ltd. & Ors. v. Anis Ahmad
holdings_chronological.holding: Offences under Sections 135–140 (theft and allied acts) are triable only by a Special Court constituted under Section 153; a Consumer Forum has no jurisdiction over any action taken under Sections 135–140.

holdings_chronological.title: Vishal Agrawal v. Chhattisgarh State Electricity Board
holdings_chronological.holding: Theft of electricity under Section 135 (punishable up to three years) is a cognizable offence; the CrPC therefore applies and it is the duty of the police to register an FIR and investigate.

holdings_chronological.title: Vishal Agrawal v. Chhattisgarh State Electricity Board
holdings_chronological.holding: The contrary High Court view (complaint-only route) does not lay down correct law; the police-FIR-competent view is approved — resolving the split.

holdings_chronological.title: Sandeep Kesarwani v. State of U.P. & 3 Others
holdings_chronological.holding: The 'assessed amount' in the sixth proviso to Section 135(1) (on payment of which supply is restored) is the amount assessed under Section 126 — textual confirmation that assessment is contemplated in theft cases.

holdings_chronological.title: Ramesh Chand v. Uttar Haryana Bijli Vitran Nigam Ltd.
holdings_chronological.holding: Sections 126 and 135 operate in different fields: Section 126 is invoked for over-consumption / unauthorised use of electricity, whereas Section 135 is invoked for theft of electricity.

holdings_chronological.title: Ramesh Chand v. Uttar Haryana Bijli Vitran Nigam Ltd.
holdings_chronological.holding: A show-cause notice / opportunity of hearing is required only where theft is suspected (broken/tampered seals, no evidence at site — per Circular 54/2007); where the theft is 'writ large' (here a dead-stop meter with a soldered wire after breaking the counter lock), no opportunity of hearing need be given before proceeding.

holdings_chronological.title: Shishir Jain v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd.
holdings_chronological.holding: Principles of natural justice apply to proceedings for unauthorised use of electricity (which may in some cases also amount to an investigation under Section 135) unless excluded by the Act expressly or by necessary implication.

holdings_chronological.title: V. Swaminathan v. Superintending Engineer, TANGEDCO
holdings_chronological.holding: Even a consumer who has compounded and paid the compounding fee should be permitted to test the correctness of the manner of computation of the civil liability fastened on him; there is a casus omissus (no forum to test the final Section 135 assessment).

holdings_chronological.title: V. Swaminathan v. Superintending Engineer, TANGEDCO
holdings_chronological.holding: Section 135 theft falls within criminal jurisprudence and mens rea is the relevant factor; Section 126 (read with the Supply Code) does not speak of criminal intent, and the assessment under it is appealable under Section 127, whereas a Section 135 assessment (Reg. 23-AA) has no statutory appeal.

holdings_chronological.title: M/s Jindal Resources Pvt. Ltd. v. Executive Engineer (Elect.), WESCO
holdings_chronological.holding: A Section 135 criminal proceeding has no bearing on a Section 126 proceeding; even an acquittal in the criminal case for a Section 135 offence does not exonerate the consumer from Section 126 civil liability.

holdings_chronological.title: M/s Jindal Resources Pvt. Ltd. v. Executive Engineer (Elect.), WESCO
holdings_chronological.holding: On the facts, the acquittal was not a clean acquittal but a benefit-of-doubt acquittal on technicality (delayed seizure, non-production of dump copy), reinforcing that it does not undo the Section 126 civil liability.

holdings_chronological.title: West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd. (WBSEDCL) v. M/s Orion Metal Pvt. Ltd.
holdings_chronological.holding: All instances of unauthorised use may not amount to theft, but theft under Section 135 falls within the definition of 'unauthorised use of electricity'; hence use through a tampered meter (Section 126(6)(b)(iii)) is unauthorised use assessable under Section 126.

holdings_chronological.title: West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd. (WBSEDCL) v. M/s Orion Metal Pvt. Ltd.
holdings_chronological.holding: Where there is no theft (only unauthorised use), no Section 135 complaint lies and the loss is assessed under Section 126(1); where the unauthorised use amounts to theft, a Section 126(1) assessment AND a Section 135 complaint may both proceed, with the Special Court determining civil liability under Section 154(5) and any excess deposit refunded.

holdings_chronological.title: West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd. (WBSEDCL) v. M/s Orion Metal Pvt. Ltd.
holdings_chronological.holding: To prove theft in a criminal proceeding, the case must be proved beyond reasonable doubt with mens rea established; such strict proof is not necessary for assessing liability under Section 126(1).

holdings_chronological.title: Rakesh Singh v. State of U.P.
holdings_chronological.holding: Unauthorised use of electricity (Explanation (b) to Section 126) is the genus of which the Section 135(1) acts are species; theft is unauthorised use done dishonestly, so a Section 126 assessment must follow whenever there is unauthorised use.

holdings_chronological.title: Rakesh Singh v. State of U.P.
holdings_chronological.holding: Neither Section 126 nor Section 135 excludes a Section 126 assessment where the unauthorised use amounts to theft; the sixth proviso to Section 135(1) itself speaks of the 'assessed amount', i.e. the amount assessed under Section 126.

holdings_chronological.title: Hasimuddin v. State of U.P.
holdings_chronological.holding: Even where an FIR is lodged under Section 135, the assessment is carried out under Section 126 (with the Section 127 appeal remedy), and the Special Court finally determines the civil liability under Section 154(6).

holdings_chronological.title: Ashok Kumar Maity v. West Bengal State Electricity Board (WBSEDCL)
holdings_chronological.holding: Unauthorised use of electricity (Section 126) is the genus and theft (Section 135) is one of the species thereunder; the two operate in different fields.

holdings_chronological.title: Ashok Kumar Maity v. West Bengal State Electricity Board (WBSEDCL)
holdings_chronological.holding: An acquittal on a Section 135 theft charge (tested on proof beyond reasonable doubt) does not ipso facto exonerate the consumer from civil liability under Section 126 (tested on the more liberal preponderance of probability).

holdings_chronological.title: Tapan Sen Majumdar v. West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd.
holdings_chronological.holding: Sections 126 and 135 operate in separate fields and parallel proceedings may run; Section 126 is civil (preponderance of probability), Section 135 is criminal (beyond reasonable doubt) — the standards of proof differ.

holdings_chronological.title: Tapan Sen Majumdar v. West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd.
holdings_chronological.holding: Where a tampered/bypassed meter is the ONLY allegation and it founds both the Section 135 prosecution and the Section 126 assessment (self-same allegation), an acquittal scot-free in the criminal case means the consumer cannot be indicted for the same charge even on a preponderance of probability.

holdings_chronological.title: Castron Technologies Ltd. v. Damodar Valley Corporation
holdings_chronological.holding: The contention that an acquittal in the Section 135 criminal case extinguishes Section 126 liability is not acceptable — a Section 135 proceeding has no bearing on a Section 126 proceeding (following Orion Metal and Seetaram Rice Mill).

holdings_chronological.title: Md. Abdul Matin v. West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd.
holdings_chronological.holding: The vires of Sections 126 and 135 is upheld; the overlap on tampering creates no double standards — where both theft and unauthorised-use ingredients are satisfied, the authorities may make a Section 126 assessment AND proceed with a Section 135 criminal trial before the Special Court.

holdings_chronological.title: Md. Abdul Matin v. West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd.
holdings_chronological.holding: A Section 126 finding does not indict a person of theft (a criminal charge); the assessing officer merely calculates the licensee's loss, and whether theft is established is left to the Special Court's full criminal trial — so no violation of Articles 19/21.

holdings_chronological.title: M/s Mohit Paper Mills Ltd. v. PVVNL
holdings_chronological.holding: For a contravention of Section 138(d), an assessment under Section 126 (or para 8.1 of the Code) is not permissible.

holdings_chronological.title: Accounts Officer, Jharkhand State Electricity Board v. Anwar Ali
holdings_chronological.holding: It was noted (relying on the Board's contention and Mam Chand) that Section 145 of the 2003 Act expressly bars the civil court from entertaining suits on matters falling under Section 126, the Act being a complete code, so assessment disputes should go to the competent authority under the Act.

holdings_chronological.title: Sh. B.L. Kantroo v. BSES Rajdhani Power Ltd.
holdings_chronological.holding: Section 145's express bar on civil-court jurisdiction operates only in respect of Section 126 (assessment) and Section 127 (appeal) matters — not theft under Section 135.

holdings_chronological.title: Sh. B.L. Kantroo v. BSES Rajdhani Power Ltd.
holdings_chronological.holding: The Electricity Act is a complete code; the civil court's jurisdiction is by necessary implication barred, and a consumer cannot approach a civil court without exhausting the alternative remedies the Act provides.

holdings_chronological.title: U.P. Power Corporation Ltd. & Ors. v. Anis Ahmad
holdings_chronological.holding: Section 145 bars civil courts over any matter an assessing officer (Section 126) or appellate authority (Section 127) may determine; read with Sections 173–174, the phrase 'other authority' does not include the Consumer Fora, which are therefore also ousted.

holdings_chronological.title: Ajmer Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Gopal Ram
holdings_chronological.holding: The question whether the civil court's jurisdiction is barred by Section 145 (matters an assessing officer under Section 126 or appellate authority under Section 127 may determine) goes to the root of the matter and must be decided before a civil court adjudicates an unauthorised-abstraction suit.

holdings_chronological.title: Ajmer Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Gopal Ram
holdings_chronological.holding: The Section 145 bar can be agitated by the respondent-defendant (licensee) in the first appeal even without filing a cross-appeal or cross-objection against the trial court's finding on jurisdiction.

holdings_chronological.title: Ajmer Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Gopal Ram
holdings_chronological.holding: Section 145 effects an absolute exclusion of the civil court's jurisdiction over unlawful-abstraction assessment matters; the appeal is remanded for that question to be decided.

holdings_chronological.title: Ashok Kumar Maity v. West Bengal State Electricity Board (WBSEDCL)
holdings_chronological.holding: Section 145 bars civil-court interference in respect of assessments under Sections 126 and 127; a Section 135 FIR instead leads to a Section 154 Special Court criminal action, with civil liability under Section 154(5) independent of and subject to the Section 126 deposit (Section 154(6)).

holdings_chronological.title: Vishal Agrawal v. Chhattisgarh State Electricity Board
holdings_chronological.holding: Section 151 enables authorised persons to file a written complaint before the Court (on which cognizance may be taken straightway), but it does not exclude the other avenue of a police FIR/investigation; the Electricity Act is not a complete machinery for how offences are dealt with, so the CrPC governs.

holdings_chronological.title: Vishal Agrawal v. Chhattisgarh State Electricity Board
holdings_chronological.holding: The amendment (proviso) to Section 151 permitting cognizance on a police report is clarificatory in nature and applies to pending matters (retrospective); notwithstanding Section 151, an FIR could be filed with the police even under the unamended provision.

holdings_chronological.title: Vishal Agrawal v. Chhattisgarh State Electricity Board
holdings_chronological.holding: The contrary High Court view (complaint-only route) does not lay down correct law; the police-FIR-competent view is approved — resolving the split.

holdings_chronological.title: BSES Rajdhani Power Ltd. v. Jagat Ram
holdings_chronological.holding: Acceptance of the compounding fee under Section 152 is deemed to amount to an acquittal within the meaning of Section 300 CrPC.

holdings_chronological.title: BSES Rajdhani Power Ltd. v. Jagat Ram
holdings_chronological.holding: After a deemed acquittal by compounding under Section 152(3), the Special Court cannot determine civil liability under Section 154(5); there is no different consequence between an acquittal after full trial and a deemed acquittal by compounding.

holdings_chronological.title: BSES Rajdhani Power Ltd. v. Jagat Ram
holdings_chronological.holding: There cannot be any compounding of the offence under Section 152 without the consent of the complainant-licensee; Section 152 permits the appropriate government to pass the compounding order but does not dispense with the complainant's consent.

holdings_chronological.title: Ramesh Chand v. Uttar Haryana Bijli Vitran Nigam Ltd.
holdings_chronological.holding: The remedy of compounding under Section 152 is available in both cases — established theft and suspected theft; accepting the compounding notice avoids trial before the Special Court, refusing it exposes the consumer to punishment and fine by that Court.

holdings_chronological.title: V. Swaminathan v. Superintending Engineer, TANGEDCO
holdings_chronological.holding: Compounding of an offence under Section 152 cannot be done 'under protest' — it is not recognised in law; if the consumer protests, the authorised officer must instead launch prosecution.

holdings_chronological.title: V. Swaminathan v. Superintending Engineer, TANGEDCO
holdings_chronological.holding: Once the consumer exercises the option to compound (an admission of guilt deemed an acquittal), there is no retracting it and he cannot canvass the correctness of the finding of guilt or claim he was compelled to compound under protest.

holdings_chronological.title: V. Swaminathan v. Superintending Engineer, TANGEDCO
holdings_chronological.holding: Even a consumer who has compounded and paid the compounding fee should be permitted to test the correctness of the manner of computation of the civil liability fastened on him; there is a casus omissus (no forum to test the final Section 135 assessment).

holdings_chronological.title: Sh. B.L. Kantroo v. BSES Rajdhani Power Ltd.
holdings_chronological.holding: Any dispute about civil liability in theft cases is impliedly excluded from the jurisdiction of the civil court by Sections 153 and 154, under which the Special Court determines such liability (acting as both civil and criminal court).

holdings_chronological.title: Sh. B.L. Kantroo v. BSES Rajdhani Power Ltd.
holdings_chronological.holding: Section 154(5) invests the Special Court with jurisdiction to determine the quantum of civil liability in theft cases; a consumer disputing a theft bill must challenge it before the Special Court, even where no criminal complaint has been filed.

holdings_chronological.title: Sh. B.L. Kantroo v. BSES Rajdhani Power Ltd.
holdings_chronological.holding: Any dispute about civil liability in theft cases is impliedly excluded from the jurisdiction of the civil court by Sections 153 and 154, under which the Special Court determines such liability (acting as both civil and criminal court).

holdings_chronological.title: M/s Shyam Lal Iron & Steel Co. v. Jharkhand State Electricity Board
holdings_chronological.holding: The remedy against a final theft assessment is before the Special Court under Section 154(5)/(6), which determines the civil liability; the writ court will not interfere.

holdings_chronological.title: Sandeep Kesarwani v. State of U.P. & 3 Others
holdings_chronological.holding: The Special Court's power under Section 154(5) to determine civil liability for theft does not preclude a Section 126 assessment; the amount 'deposited' referred to in Section 154(6) is the amount assessed under Section 126, there being no other provision for such a deposit.

holdings_chronological.title: BSES Rajdhani Power Ltd. v. Jagat Ram
holdings_chronological.holding: Civil liability under Section 154(5) is defined (Explanation) as loss 'due to the commission of an offence', so its determination must necessarily be preceded by a positive determination of the commission of the offence.

holdings_chronological.title: BSES Rajdhani Power Ltd. v. Jagat Ram
holdings_chronological.holding: After a deemed acquittal by compounding under Section 152(3), the Special Court cannot determine civil liability under Section 154(5); there is no different consequence between an acquittal after full trial and a deemed acquittal by compounding.

holdings_chronological.title: BSES Rajdhani Power Ltd. v. Jagat Ram
holdings_chronological.holding: The Special Court combines both criminal and civil jurisdictions, so the view that a criminal court cannot determine civil liability is incorrect; but its conclusion that no civil liability can be determined after a compounding-acquittal is correct.

holdings_chronological.title: Ramesh Chand v. Uttar Haryana Bijli Vitran Nigam Ltd.
holdings_chronological.holding: Section 126 cannot be applied to assess the amount to be charged for theft of electricity; the civil liability for theft is measured under the Section 154(5) formula (twice the tariff for the twelve months preceding detection, or the exact period of theft if determined, whichever is less), subject to final adjudication by the Special Court.

holdings_chronological.title: M/s Jindal Resources Pvt. Ltd. v. Executive Engineer (Elect.), WESCO
holdings_chronological.holding: The amount 'deposited by the consumer' in Section 154(6) is the amount deposited under Section 126 (there being no other deposit provision for theft), so the Section 154(5) Special Court does not oust the Section 126 assessment; the argument that only the Special Court may assess is rejected.

holdings_chronological.title: West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd. (WBSEDCL) v. M/s Orion Metal Pvt. Ltd.
holdings_chronological.holding: The Section 126(1) assessment power and the Section 154(5) Special Court power to determine civil liability are not parallel to each other; the High Court erred in holding that both proceedings cannot operate parallelly.

holdings_chronological.title: West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd. (WBSEDCL) v. M/s Orion Metal Pvt. Ltd.
holdings_chronological.holding: Where there is no theft (only unauthorised use), no Section 135 complaint lies and the loss is assessed under Section 126(1); where the unauthorised use amounts to theft, a Section 126(1) assessment AND a Section 135 complaint may both proceed, with the Special Court determining civil liability under Section 154(5) and any excess deposit refunded.

holdings_chronological.title: West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd. (WBSEDCL) v. M/s Orion Metal Pvt. Ltd.
holdings_chronological.holding: Merely because the Special Court is empowered to determine civil liability under Section 154(5) where a complaint is lodged, it cannot be said that the authorities have no power to make a Section 126 assessment.

holdings_chronological.title: Rakesh Singh v. State of U.P.
holdings_chronological.holding: The 'amount deposited by the consumer' in Section 154(6) is the amount deposited under Section 126 — there being no other deposit provision for theft — so Section 126 assessment and the Special Court's Section 154(5) determination coexist.

holdings_chronological.title: Tapan Sen Majumdar v. West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd.
holdings_chronological.holding: The Explanation to Section 154(6) ('civil liability') refers to the liability determined by the Special Court under Section 154(5) for theft, not to the amount raised as a provisional assessment under Section 126.

holdings_chronological.title: U.P. Power Corporation Ltd. & Ors. v. Anis Ahmad
holdings_chronological.holding: Although Sections 173–175 and Section 3 CPA save consumer rights and give the CPA primacy on true inconsistency, they do not vest a Consumer Forum with power to adjudicate a Section 126 assessment or a Sections 135–140 offence, because such acts are neither a 'complaint' (s.2(1)(c)) nor a 'deficiency in service' (s.2(1)(o),(g)) under the CPA.

holdings_chronological.title: K.C. Ninan v. Kerala State Electricity Board
holdings_chronological.holding: The rule-making power under Section 181 read with Section 50 is wide enough to enable the regulatory commission to provide for a statutory CHARGE on the premises, even absent a charge-creating provision in the plenary statute.

holdings_chronological.title: M/s Prem Cottex v. Uttar Haryana Bijli Vitran Nigam Ltd.
holdings_chronological.holding: A consumer forum must, at the threshold, find whether there was any deficiency in service before it can test the licensee's recovery against Section 56.

holdings_chronological.title: M/s Shyam Lal Iron & Steel Co. v. Jharkhand State Electricity Board
holdings_chronological.holding: The suspected-theft safeguards in Clause 15.8(x)-(xv) (continued supply, provisional assessment, show-cause, 75%-consumption drop) have no application to a clear theft case, which is governed by Clause 15.8(i)-(ix).

holdings_chronological.title: Rakesh Singh v. State of U.P.
holdings_chronological.holding: The U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 (Clause 8.1) requires a provisional assessment bill and final assessment even in Section 135 theft cases, confirming that assessment for theft is made under Section 126.

holdings_chronological.title: Bihar State Electricity Board v. Kishori Devi
holdings_chronological.holding: Where urgent action is needed to protect the Board's property and prevent ongoing pilferage, the audi alteram partem rule is dispensed with; disconnection without notice is valid and not violative of natural justice or Article 14.

holdings_chronological.title: Bihar State Electricity Board v. Kishori Devi
holdings_chronological.holding: Although natural justice is excluded at the disconnection stage, the determination of the value of energy consumed and the assessment of compensation must be made after giving the affected person an opportunity of hearing — that requirement is read into the clause even though it is silent.
